title: Incidence and Nature of Antidepressant Discontinuation Symptoms: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
authors: Kalfas M, Tsapekos D, Butler M, McCutcheon RA, Pillinger T, Strawbridge R, et al.
followUp: 1 day to 52 weeks; main analyses at 1 and 2 weeks after stopping
population: 50 randomised trials in adults stopping an antidepressant, against placebo discontinuation or antidepressant continuation; most prior treatment courses were short-term
funder: not stated: the article information read in PubMed Central and in the archived journal page carries no funding statement. Data from 9 of the 49 analysed trials were provided by Lundbeck, Takeda, Lilly and Pfizer through Vivli.
authorConflicts: Several authors reported fees from manufacturers of antidepressants or other psychiatric drugs (Boehringer Ingelheim, Janssen, Lundbeck, Viatris, Eli Lilly, Otsuka, Servier, Takeda and others); one author reported honoraria for articles on discontinuation symptoms in journal supplements sponsored by Eli Lilly in 1997, 2000 and 2006.
result: At 1 week after stopping, DESS scores were higher than with placebo or continuation (SMD 0.31, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.39; 11 trials, 3915 participants), about 1.08 more symptoms; at 2 weeks SMD 0.13 (0.05 to 0.21). In placebo-controlled trials (4357 stopping an antidepressant, 2801 stopping placebo), dizziness occurred in 7.5% against 1.8% (OR 5.52, 3.81 to 8.01; risk difference 6.24%), nausea OR 3.16, vertigo OR 6.40, nervousness OR 3.15. The authors concluded that the mean number of symptoms was below the threshold for a clinically significant discontinuation syndrome and that mood worsening was not associated with discontinuation (5 trials). A published reader comment by Horowitz noted that the DESS trials followed 8 to 12 weeks of exposure.
